Applied anatomy of the femoral triangle and femoral canal, relevant to femoral hernia

brief.scenario: Mr Omar Thistlewood, 57, has a groin swelling that becomes more prominent when standing.
brief.task: Take a focused history and distinguish a hernia from other causes of a groin lump.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Establish reducibility and posture-dependence first, then screen for obstruction or strangulation before moving to risk factors.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Not every groin lump is an inguinal hernia; lymph nodes, a saphena varix, a hydrocele of the cord and a lipoma all sit in the differential.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Can you tell me what happens to the lump when you stand up, cough or lie down?"

grid.label: Opening and reducibility
grid.fail: Doesn't establish whether the lump is reducible or how it relates to posture.
grid.pass: Establishes onset, progression, and relation to standing, coughing, lifting and straining.
grid.high: Specifically asks whether it fully disappears lying flat, distinguishing a simple reducible swelling from one that doesn't reduce.

grid.label: Obstruction and strangulation features
grid.fail: Doesn't ask about pain, vomiting, distension or bowel habit.
grid.pass: Asks about pain, tenderness, vomiting, abdominal distension and bowel obstruction symptoms.
grid.high: Specifically asks about a painful, irreducible lump, distinguishing that from a comfortable, reducible one.

grid.label: Previous surgery and risk factors
grid.fail: Omits previous surgery, previous hernia or occupation.
grid.pass: Asks about previous groin or abdominal surgery, previous hernia or repair, occupation and heavy lifting.
grid.high: Asks about urinary symptoms, constipation and, where relevant, pregnancy history as factors that raise intra-abdominal pressure.

grid.label: Examination plan
grid.fail: Plans to examine only lying supine.
grid.pass: Plans to examine standing and supine, including cough impulse and reducibility, assessing both groins.
grid.high: States a groin lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle raises the possibility of a femoral hernia, but that examination is needed to confirm.

grid.label: Differential diagnosis
grid.fail: Assumes every groin lump is an inguinal hernia.
grid.pass: Lists inguinal hernia, femoral hernia, lymph node, saphena varix, hydrocele of the cord, lipoma and vascular lesions as differentials.
grid.high: Notes a previous incarceration or strangulation episode would raise concern for recurrent or complicated hernia.

grid.label: Managing a painful, irreducible lump
grid.fail: Would attempt forceful reduction of a painful, irreducible lump without urgent senior assessment.
grid.pass: Recognises a painful, irreducible lump needs urgent senior surgical assessment rather than forceful reduction.
grid.high: Explains an acutely painful irreducible hernia with obstructive or systemic features is a surgical emergency.

grid.label: Presentation and next steps
grid.fail: Presents findings without a differential or a plan.
grid.pass: Presents a focused summary, a differential, and a plan for examination and further assessment.
grid.high: States history and examination usually strongly suggest the diagnosis, with imaging reserved for genuine diagnostic uncertainty.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: So it's a hernia. Next question.

fail.text: I didn't think to ask that.

fail.text: I don't think that's relevant here.

fail.text: If it were painful and wouldn't go back in?

fail.speaker: candidate

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello Mr Thistlewood, I'm Dr Patel. Can you tell me when you first noticed the lump, and what happens to it when you stand, cough or lie down?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Mr Thistlewood: "It comes out when I cough and usually goes when I lie down."

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Is it painful or tender, and have you had any vomiting, tummy bloating or change in your bowel habit?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Mr Thistlewood: "No pain, no vomiting, bowels normal."

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Have you had any groin or abdominal surgery, or a hernia before? What's your job, and does it involve heavy lifting?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Mr Thistlewood: "No previous surgery. I do a lot of manual lifting at work."

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd like to examine him standing and lying down, checking for a cough impulse and whether it reduces, and examine both groins.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Most likely an inguinal hernia, but I'd also consider a femoral hernia, an enlarged lymph node, a saphena varix, a hydrocele of the cord or a lipoma.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: If it were painful and irreducible?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I wouldn't force reduction; that would need urgent senior surgical assessment.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A reducible, cough-impulse-positive groin swelling with no pain or obstructive symptoms, most consistent with an inguinal hernia. I'd examine standing and supine and discuss elective repair.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello Mr Thistlewood, I'm Dr Patel. When did you first notice it, and does it fully disappear when you lie flat, or does something remain?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Mr Thistlewood: "It disappears completely lying down."

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Is it painful, tender, or has it ever got stuck out and not gone back? Any vomiting, distension or change in bowel habit?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Mr Thistlewood: "No, comfortable, and always goes back."

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Any groin or abdominal surgery, previous hernia or repair, occupation with heavy lifting, urinary symptoms or constipation that might raise pressure inside the tummy?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Mr Thistlewood: "None of that, but I do heavy manual work."

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll examine him standing and supine, checking cough impulse and reducibility, and compare both groins. If it sat below and lateral to the pubic tubercle I'd think femoral hernia, but I'd confirm that on examination rather than history alone.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Differential includes inguinal hernia, femoral hernia, lymph node, saphena varix, hydrocele of the cord, lipoma and vascular lesions. I'd also ask about any previous incarceration or strangulation, which would raise concern for recurrent or complex disease.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: If it were painful and irreducible?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's an emergency if there are obstructive or systemic features, I wouldn't attempt forceful reduction and would escalate for urgent senior assessment.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A cough-impulse-positive, fully reducible groin swelling with no pain or obstructive symptoms, in a man doing heavy manual work: most consistent with an inguinal hernia. History and examination usually make the diagnosis strongly likely, and I'd reserve imaging for genuine diagnostic uncertainty.

failures.move: Attempting forceful reduction of a painful, irreducible groin lump.
failures.consequence: Risks worsening strangulated or incarcerated bowel; needs urgent senior surgical assessment instead.

failures.move: Assuming every groin lump is an inguinal hernia.
failures.consequence: A femoral hernia, node, or vascular lesion needing different management is missed.

failures.move: Not asking about obstructive or strangulation symptoms.
failures.consequence: A complicated hernia needing urgent assessment is missed.
A reducible hernia may not be visible or palpable, and the diagnosis is missed or delayed.

recovery.line: I should also examine him standing, since the swelling and cough impulse may only be apparent then.

recovery.when: Asked what would concern you most
recovery.line: A lump that's painful and won't reduce, especially with vomiting or distension, because that suggests strangulation.

knowledge.fact: History and physical examination are central to diagnosing a groin hernia; imaging is reserved for genuine diagnostic uncertainty.
Management considers symptoms, patient factors and hernia type; an acutely painful, irreducible hernia with obstructive or systemic features needs urgent assessment.

recall.think: Is this a simple reducible hernia, or a painful irreducible one needing urgent assessment?
recall.say: "A reducible, cough-impulse-positive groin swelling is most consistent with an inguinal hernia."
do: Examine standing and supine, both groins
recall.trap: Not every groin lump is a hernia, and lying supine alone can miss a reducible one.
recall.finish: Elective repair discussion if simple and reducible; urgent senior assessment if painful and irreducible.

partner.opening: Please take a focused history from Mr Thistlewood. I'll ask you some questions at the end.
partner.actorBrief: You are Omar Thistlewood, 57, a warehouse operative. The groin lump comes out when you cough or stand and goes fully when you lie flat. No pain, no vomiting, bowels normal. No previous groin or abdominal surgery. Heavy manual lifting at work. No urinary symptoms or constipation. If asked about previous strangulation, say no.

reveals.finding: Comes out coughing or standing; disappears fully lying flat.

reveals.trigger: Asks about pain or obstructive symptoms
reveals.finding: No pain, no vomiting, no distension, bowels normal.

reveals.trigger: Asks about surgery, occupation or risk factors
reveals.finding: No previous surgery or hernia; heavy manual lifting at work.

push.question: Would you image him before deciding on surgery?
push.expect: Not usually; history and examination make the diagnosis, with imaging reserved for genuine uncertainty.

push.question: What makes a groin lump an emergency?
push.expect: Painful irreducibility, obstruction, strangulation features or systemic deterioration.

push.question: How would you tell a femoral hernia from an inguinal one on history?
push.expect: History alone can't reliably distinguish them; a lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle raises suspicion of femoral hernia, confirmed on examination.

curveballs.prompt: He says the lump has become painful today and won't go back in.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Treats as a possible incarcerated or strangulated hernia: does not force reduction, arranges urgent senior surgical assessment.

curveballs.prompt: He mentions he's also been vomiting and hasn't opened his bowels for two days.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Raises concern for bowel obstruction from the hernia; urgent surgical assessment, keep nil by mouth, consider IV fluids.

curveballs.prompt: He says his father had a hernia repaired that later came back.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Notes recurrence risk factors, but continues to build the current picture from his own symptoms and examination rather than family history alone.

curveballs.prompt: The lump is soft, non-reducible, and lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Raises concern for a femoral hernia, which carries a higher strangulation risk, and prompts more urgent assessment.
